lede: Living things react to change, and in an animal two systems carry the message. Nerve impulses travel fast along neurones and the effect is soon over; hormones travel more slowly in the blood and last longer. The brain and spinal cord co-ordinate what happens in between.
can: Compare the nervous and hormonal systems on speed and duration.
Put stimulus, receptor, CNS, effector and response in order.
Tell a voluntary action from a reflex one.

md: Your body sends messages two ways: down a nerve, fast and soon over, or through the blood as a hormone, slower and longer-lasting. The brain and spinal cord sit in the middle of both.

alt: A four-row table comparing the nervous and hormonal systems: what carries the message (nerve impulses against hormones), how it travels (along neurones against in the blood), the speed of response (fast against slower) and how long it lasts (short-lived against longer-lasting).

md:
**The nervous system** sends **electrical nerve impulses** along **neurones**. It is **fast** and its effects are **short-lived** — you pull your hand back and a second later it is over.
**The hormonal system** sends **chemical hormones** in the **blood**. It is **slower**, because the blood takes time to carry them round, but the effects are **longer-lasting**.

prompt: How does the speed of a hormonal response compare with a nervous response?
explain: Slower — hormones travel in the blood, which takes far longer than an impulse along a neurone. The outcome names speed specifically, so this comparison is always available.

title: Why one system is fast and the other lasts
md: A nerve impulse runs along a neurone that already reaches its target, so it arrives at once and stops when the impulses stop. A hormone travels all round the body in the blood, and keeps working until the blood clears it.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Nervous System"
why: Six minutes covering the CNS, receptors, effectors and the difference between voluntary and reflex actions — the whole of this topic in one pass. Watch it, then answer the question underneath without looking back.

prompt: The central nervous system is made up of the brain and the ______ ______ .
explain: The brain and the spinal cord — those two and nothing else. The nerves running to your fingers are not part of the CNS.

md:
**Receptor** — a structure that detects a change (a stimulus): light receptors in the eye, touch and pain receptors in the skin.
**CNS** — the brain and spinal cord, which **co-ordinate** the response: they decide what should happen.
**Effector** — the thing that carries it out. On this specification an effector is a **muscle** or a **gland**, and nothing else.

prompt: A receptor in the eye detects a change. What is it called?
explain: The stimulus is the change; the response is what follows.

title: March 2026 B1 Higher Q6(b)(i) and Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q4(b)(ii)
md: In Summer 2025, asked to name an effector, **many candidates correctly stated muscle**. In March 2026 the same idea was set as a labelling task and it went far less well: examiners saw **the pin, the hand and individual nerves** all labelled as the effector. The test is simple — an effector is the thing that *does* the response, and on this specification it is always a muscle or a gland.

prompt: You touch something hot and your arm muscle pulls your hand away. What is the effector?
explain: The muscle — it carries out the response. The hand is the body part that moves and the hot object is the stimulus.

alt: A three-row table comparing voluntary and reflex actions: conscious control (yes, you decide, against no, automatic), speed (slower against very fast) and an example (picking up a pen against blinking at dust).

md: A **voluntary** action is one you **consciously decide** to make: the brain is involved and it takes longer. A **reflex** action is **automatic** and **not under conscious control**, and it is **much faster** — a reflex might take about 0.05 s while a voluntary response to the same signal takes about 0.25 s, which is 5 times longer. That speed is the point of a reflex: it protects you before you have had time to think.

prompt: A reflex takes 0.05 s and a voluntary response takes 0.25 s. How many times longer is the voluntary response?
explain: 0.25 ÷ 0.05 = 5. 'How many times' means divide; 'how much longer' would mean subtract, giving 0.20 s.

title: PhET: Neuron

task: Fire a nerve impulse and watch how quickly it crosses the screen. Then write one sentence explaining why a message carried this way reaches a muscle faster than a hormone carried in the blood.

prompt: Which of these is a reflex action?
options: blinking when dust blows into your eye
answer: blinking when dust blows into your eye
explain: Blinking happens without you choosing it and it happens fast. The other two are conscious decisions, so they are voluntary.

md:
Compare the **nervous** and **hormonal** systems on speed and duration.
Name the two parts of the **CNS**.
Put **stimulus, receptor, CNS, effector, response** in order.
Tell a **voluntary** action from a **reflex**.

Short recall marks scattered through a nervous-system question: an effector named, the difference in speed between the two systems, the two parts of the CNS, and one difference between a voluntary and a reflex action. The schemes are strict about the comparison: *different* is not one, and *quicker* without naming both systems is half of one.
